article.title: PyPI's New Security Tab Rates Every Release's Provenance, Reigniting a Debate Over Unequal Access to Trusted Publishing
article.summary: PyPI's redesigned project pages now grade every release's provenance, and a community debate is testing whether the new signals favor projects on supported CI platforms.
article.body_markdown:
## Background

The Python Package Index redesigned its project pages, adding a dedicated Security tab that grades each release's provenance, according to [Help Net Security](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/11/09/pypi-security-tab-release-attestations/). The tab shows whether a release's files carry digital attestations, which the outlet describes as information verifying how a file was published or built. A release has "full provenance" when every file has at least one attestation, and PyPI distinguishes two attestation types: a PyPI Publish attestation identifies the Trusted Publisher that uploaded the file, while an SLSA Build Provenance attestation links the file back to its source commit, build platform and build instructions, per [Help Net Security](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/11/09/pypi-security-tab-release-attestations/).

Trusted Publishing lets a project authenticate to PyPI directly from a continuing-integration provider's OpenID Connect identity, without a long-lived API token. PyPI currently approves a limited set of such providers. That limitation is the center of a disagreement that opened on [discuss.python.org](https://discuss.python.org/t/pypis-new-security-indicators-and-unequal-access-to-trusted-publishing/109930) the day after the redesign went live, when community member Ricardo Newbery asked whether PyPI "present[s] stronger security signals for publishing workflows that only a limited set of approved infrastructure providers can currently support." William Woodruff, who worked on the original Trusted Publishing and attestation designs but, by his own account in the thread, was "not directly involved in the recent UI/presentation work" and spoke only for himself, replied in the same thread, and Pillow co-maintainer Hugo van Kemenade added a concrete example from his own project's release history. The exchange is the Herald's focus here because it surfaces a disagreement over what a security-signaling redesign actually signals, not because either side has reached a conclusion.

## Current situation

### What the Security tab shows, and what it warns about

A release has "no provenance" when none of its files carry an attestation, and Nicole Harris, a PyPI design contributor, told [Help Net Security](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/11/09/pypi-security-tab-release-attestations/) that this "is common for older releases and projects that have yet to configure Trusted Publishing," adding that "such a release isn't necessarily malicious, since the missing attestation only means its origin can't be cryptographically verified." For releases in between, PyPI "warns users when only some files in a release have attestations or when files in the same release come from different repositories or build systems," and it also warns "when a release comes from a different repository or workflow than a previous version, or when a project that previously provided attestations stops doing so," the outlet reports. It adds that such a workflow change "often has a legitimate explanation, such as an organization renaming itself or moving its repository, though it may signal a compromised pipeline or an account takeover."

Woodruff, posting on discuss.python.org, described the design as resting on four underlying states: a project that has never had attestations, a project that has them, a project that had them and lost them, and a project with only some files attested in a given release. He wrote that the first two states are "neutral," while the latter two carry a warning, "despite" the never-attested state being "logically as un-protected" as the lost-attestation state. He called this asymmetry intentional: flagging a project for never adopting attestations, he wrote, "would effectively be punishing users for never adopting attestations, which is not the goal."

### A concrete test case: Pillow's one flagged release

Van Kemenade, who co-maintains the imaging library Pillow, posted his project's own history as a test of that design. Pillow's releases moved from "No provenance" to "Full provenance" in October 2024, he wrote, and every release since has carried full provenance except one: version 11.3.0, released in July 2025, which the Security tab flags as "Incomplete provenance." He quoted PyPI's own warning text for that release: "20 of 106 release files were uploaded without provenance metadata." Looking closer, he found that 86 of those files were uploaded through GitHub Actions and link to the originating commit and workflow, while 20 manylinux2014 and aarch64 wheels were uploaded two days later outside that pipeline, after the project's build tool, cibuildwheel, changed its defaults and dropped those wheel variants from the automated release. Pillow's maintainers built the missing wheels separately and uploaded them manually, which left them without an attestation and triggered the warning — a sequence he described as benign and already documented in the project's own GitHub issue tracker.

### How common full provenance actually is

A developer writing on [dev.to](https://dev.to/frankchu/61100-top-pypi-packages-ship-full-provenance-3h40), frank chu, measured how far adoption of the new provenance states has spread among PyPI's most-used packages. Checking each of the 100 most-downloaded packages on the index on November 14, 2026, chu found that "61 of the 100 most-downloaded packages on PyPI now ship with full provenance," while "the other 39 — including boto3, the single most-downloaded package on the index — ship with no provenance at all." Other named packages without provenance in chu's count included botocore, s3transfer, FastAPI, httpx, ruff, setuptools, PyYAML, protobuf and rich. Chu also reported that within this top-100 sample, the split was binary: "Nobody in the top 100 has a half-signed release," meaning none of the sampled packages carried PyPI's "incomplete" or "inconsistent" provenance states at the time chu checked them in mid-November 2026. Pillow's one incomplete-provenance release, by contrast, dates to July 2025 and had already been superseded by later full-provenance releases by the time of chu's snapshot, which is consistent with chu finding no incomplete-provenance releases among the current top 100.

### Why some providers are missing

Newbery's post pointed to a specific, open request: a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/pypi/warehouse/issues/19786) asking PyPI to add Codeberg, a code-hosting platform built on the Forgejo software, as a Trusted Publishing provider. The issue's author wrote that they were "migration my repos to codeberg" and wanted the same Trusted Publisher support GitHub already has, so they could complete the move. A separate, longer-standing [GitHub issue](https://github.com/pypi/warehouse/issues/18889), opened by GitHub user miketheman in October 2025, serves as a meta-tracker whose stated purpose is to "Collect all related requests for adding Trusted Publishing support for a given CI provider." Woodruff, replying to Newbery, said PyPI "wants to add more Trusted Publisher providers" but is held back by two factors: limited maintainer review time, and security concerns about specific identity providers. He named Codeberg and other Forgejo-based forges specifically, writing that they "currently store IdP private key materials on disk," which he called "an unacceptable risk to PyPI's users" in his own assessment. He also said attestations are not tied to any particular CI provider in principle — they are built on Trusted Publishing today only because, in his words, that "was the easiest way to provide a default experience" — and pointed to a separate, unresolved proposal for email-based attestations that would not require a CI/CD provider at all.

## Implications

Newbery's post frames the stakes as he sees them: "PyPI may unintentionally create a two-tier system in which projects using approved, predominantly commercial infrastructure receive stronger positive security signals, while projects committed to independent infrastructure or alternative release-security practices are placed at a disadvantage." That is Newbery's own characterization of the risk, not a finding PyPI or Woodruff endorsed in the thread; Woodruff's reply defended the current design's asymmetry as intentional rather than disputing that a project without supported infrastructure receives a different signal than one with it.

What the two participants agree on, based on the thread, is narrower than what divides them: both describe attestations as optional in principle, and Woodruff stated plainly that "there is no foreseeable future in which installers (like pip and uv) can impose attestations as a requirement." Where they part is on effect rather than intent — Newbery's concern is that a prominent, color-coded warning can function as de facto pressure toward supported platforms regardless of whether PyPI intends to require attestations outright, and he raised that concern explicitly even while crediting Woodruff's own prior statement that PyPI has no plan to make attestations mandatory.

The Pillow and top-100 data points, read together, illustrate the range of situations the new display now surfaces without resolving the dispute over whether the display is well-calibrated. Pillow's single flagged release shows the warning firing on a project with an established, fully-documented Trusted Publishing setup for an incidental, well-understood reason — a change in a build tool's defaults, not a security lapse. Chu's count of 61 full-provenance packages against 39 without — a ratio the Herald calculates as roughly three to two — shows that, among the top 100 packages, adoption is still split rather than near-universal, with widely used packages such as boto3 on the no-provenance side; none of those packages, in chu's sample, show a warning state at all, since no-provenance is one of the two states Woodruff described as neutral. Whether PyPI's open requests for additional Trusted Publishing providers, including the Codeberg request Newbery cited, are resolved before or after the new display becomes more widely visible to users is a question the cited sources leave open: both of the GitHub issues on Trusted Publishing provider expansion remain open as of this writing, with no resolution date stated in either.
